threat_of_the_week.title: One attacker's AI agents broke into about 100 company websites
threat_of_the_week.tldr: NorForge researcher Snorre Fagerland found exposed panels showing a Chinese-speaking operator steering Claude Code and DeepSeek agents through the open-source Cairn platform to break into company sites. Reuters named Deere, SharkNinja and Cummins among about 100 victims, at roughly 50 dollars in AI tokens per success.
threat_of_the_week.smb: Turn on automatic updates for your website platform and plugins, and rotate the admin and hosting passwords for any site you have not touched in months.

items.title: UK cyber agency: AI will speed up ransomware and phishing within two years
items.tldr: The UK's NCSC said hostile groups will very likely use AI within two years to scale up ransomware, phishing and attacks on known flaws, with AI-powered ransomware likely to hit UK critical infrastructure by 2028. Its chief said the danger is old weaknesses that AI now finds faster.
items.smb: Take any system off the internet that does not need to be online, and treat patching and multi-factor login as the starting point, not the finish line.

items.source: Help Net Security, on Google and Mandiant research
items.title: Stolen AI access is leaving companies with cloud bills of up to 1 million dollars
items.tldr: Google Threat Intelligence and Mandiant describe criminals breaking into company cloud accounts and reselling the AI model access through cheap underground subscriptions. In one case a stolen key made over 500,000 model calls in under eight hours, and some victims saw charges above 100,000 dollars in a single day.
items.smb: Set billing alerts and spending caps on every cloud and AI account, and get an alert whenever an AI service is switched on or re-enabled.

items.title: Haddix releases SpikeStrip, decoys that trip up AI pentesting agents
items.tldr: Jason Haddix of Arcanum released SpikeStrip, an experimental open-source project that hides fake vulnerability leads, prompt injection decoys and reasoning traps in a website's code comments. The aim is to waste the time and compute of AI hacking agents that scan a site, without changing how the site works.
items.smb: Assume AI agents are scanning your public website, and review its page source for comments that reveal internal paths, software versions or credentials.

items.title: Northflank breach: customers' stored AI API keys used by attackers
items.tldr: Cloud hosting platform Northflank says an attacker reached secrets held in its control plane on October 30, and several customers then saw their AI provider keys used without permission. The company told every customer to treat all stored environment variables as stolen and to rotate them.
items.smb: Rotate any AI, cloud and payment keys stored with a hosting platform, set spending caps with your AI providers, and check their usage logs for charges you don't recognise.

items.source: Help Net Security, on Sophos research
items.title: Ransomware group had AI coding agents do most of its hands-on hacking
items.tldr: Sophos found that the GOLD OGRE group, behind Aur0ra ransomware, gave AI coding agents stolen VPN logins and let them map networks, hunt for passwords and move between machines with little human input. The attackers passed off the work as authorised red-team testing, and three victims later appeared on its leak site.
items.smb: Put phishing-resistant MFA on your VPN and remote access, patch internet-facing devices first, and make sure someone acts on endpoint security alerts within hours.

items.source: Help Net Security, on Cisco Talos research
items.title: VOLTA infostealer sends stolen data to an AI model to rank what is worth selling
items.tldr: Cisco Talos found a Windows password stealer, VOLTA-AUTODOXER, that builds a profile of each victim and asks AI models through OpenRouter to rank their accounts and wallets by resale value. If one model refuses, it falls back to others, and buyers order custom copies that report back over Telegram.
items.smb: Turn on MFA for email and finance accounts, stop staff saving work passwords in browsers on shared or personal PCs, and use a password manager instead.

items.title: Schneier: AI is finding critical bugs faster than ever recorded
items.tldr: Bruce Schneier pointed to an estimate that about 3 percent of all critical software flaws ever logged were found in the past month, a pace that could add roughly a quarter to the all-time total this year. He agreed that AI-driven bug finding has changed the landscape.
items.smb: Expect more patches, more often: turn on automatic updates where you can and set a weekly slot to apply the rest.

items.title: Unit 42: likely AI-written scripts used to spy on government Linux servers
items.tldr: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 tracked an unidentified group, CL-UNK-1211, that used web shells, a Go-based trojan called SysGoRAT and password-stealing tricks against government-linked Linux servers. Many of its scripts read like chatbot answers, which suggests AI wrote or ran them.
items.smb: Check your Linux servers for unexpected PHP files in web folders and changes to .bashrc, and move any passwords stored in config files into a secrets manager.

items.title: Miessler: attackers have the AI edge for now, so cover the basics fast
items.tldr: Daniel Miessler argues that AI currently helps attackers more than defenders, because they can turn a new technique into an attack within hours while most companies take weeks. His answer is a short list of cheap basics: know every system you run, hide what does not need to be public, and plan for a vendor breach.
items.smb: Write down every website, app, API and database you expose to the internet, then put anything that does not need to be public behind a private network or tunnel.

items.title: Willison highlights Kingsbury's warning that AI makes software maturity easy to fake
items.tldr: Simon Willison shared a passage from Kyle Kingsbury's Jepsen report on ParticleDB arguing that LLMs erode trust in documentation and the companies behind software. Polished docs and tidy repos used to signal a mature project, and now they can be generated in minutes.
items.smb: Before adopting a new open-source tool or vendor, check its release history, issue tracker and real users rather than trusting polished docs alone.

items.title: Built-in browsers in AI coding assistants let web pages reach the developer's machine
items.tldr: Forever Security showed that the embedded browsers in Cursor, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex, VS Code and Claude Desktop could be abused to run commands, fake a sign-in page or read files such as SSH keys and .env secrets. Cursor and Copilot have fixed their issues; Codex and VS Code were still unpatched at publication.
items.smb: Tell developers not to click links or setup buttons their AI assistant opens from unfamiliar projects, and keep API keys out of plain .env files on laptops.

items.title: Hugging Face cryptominer campaign returns days after takedown
items.tldr: Pluto Security tracked 31 fake Qwen2 test models on Hugging Face that install a cryptominer, and sometimes a reverse shell, when loaded with trust_remote_code enabled. A second wave appeared under new accounts days after the first takedown, and its main model passed platform scans while reaching over 28,000 downloads.
items.smb: Turn off trust_remote_code by default and only load models from publishers you have vetted on GPU servers.

items.title: Web host 123 Reg says an AI-driven attack read customer contact data
items.tldr: UK web host 123 Reg disclosed that a September intruder read customer names, phone numbers, VAT numbers and account details, and AI attack tooling was found on the attacker's servers. It suspects a China-linked group tied to the ARTEX agentic hacking framework; that link is not independently confirmed.
items.smb: Warn staff that scammers may now know which hosting products you buy, and turn on two-step verification at your domain and hosting provider.

items.title: Wiz: nine AI developer platforms breached in October, stolen AI keys resold
items.tldr: Wiz tied a month of breaches at AI developer platforms, including Fireworks AI, Railway, Warp and Northflank, to attackers taking customers' stored environment variables. Stolen AI keys were tested within about 30 minutes and later ran up more than 2.5 million Bedrock calls through resale pools.
items.smb: Rotate any AI or cloud keys stored on a hosting or AI platform at the issuer, and set budget alerts on each provider account.

items.title: Seven telltale signs that an AI agent, not a person, is running an intrusion
items.tldr: Wiz described patterns it now sees in real attacks where AI agents do the hands-on work, such as machine-paced retries, plain-language plans left in tools and trying many paths at once. It says these attacks are noisy rather than stealthy, which gives defenders a chance to spot them.
items.smb: Ask your IT or MSP whether alerts would catch a burst of rapid, repeated login or command attempts, and test it once.

items.title: Survey: most firms run AI agents, few keep a full list of their AI tools
items.tldr: A Wiz survey of 100 IT and security leaders found 55 percent deploy autonomous AI agents but only 17 percent keep a complete inventory of their AI systems. About half found unapproved AI apps in use over the past year.
items.smb: List every AI tool and agent your staff use, who owns each one and what data it can reach, and review it each quarter.

items.source: The Hacker News, on Parameter research
items.title: A shared ChatGPT link could run attacker code and read private chats
items.tldr: Researchers at Parameter found that a crafted ChatGPT share link could slip attacker code into the main ChatGPT page and read the private conversations of anyone who opened it. OpenAI fixed it server-side by October 26 and no real-world abuse was reported.
items.smb: Treat unexpected shared AI chat links like any unknown link, and tell staff not to open ones that arrive unprompted.

items.title: Chainalysis says an attacker using agentic AI techniques reached its internal tools
items.tldr: Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis disclosed that an outside actor, detected using what it called offensive agentic techniques, accessed internal tools and customer names, emails, user IDs and role labels. It says investigation data, credentials and session tokens were not reached.
items.smb: Warn staff that leaked names and roles fuel targeted phishing, and require a second check before acting on unusual email requests.

items.title: DOJ asks for a privacy watchdog before Character.AI chat logs can be sold
items.tldr: The Justice Department asked a bankruptcy court to appoint a consumer privacy ombudsman because Character.AI's privacy policy may allow users' chat histories to be sold to a buyer. The DOJ says that conflicts with what the chatbot tells its roughly 12 million monthly users.
items.smb: Review what your AI vendors' terms say happens to your prompts and files if they are sold or go bankrupt, and keep sensitive data out of tools that are unclear.

items.source: The Hacker News, on Cursor and OpenSourceMalware
items.title: Fake Claude Code update on Cursor's marketplace planted an SSH backdoor
items.tldr: For about 11 hours on October 29, Cursor's extension marketplace served a trojanized Claude Code update that added an attacker SSH key, set up persistence and sent host details out. Cursor says up to 5,000 users may have received it and has pulled it; the official 2.1.314 release is clean.
items.smb: Check developer machines for an svc-telemetry key in authorized_keys, then rotate any credentials stored on affected laptops.

items.title: China-linked group used the ARTEX AI framework against 200+ organizations
items.tldr: CrowdStrike says a Chinese state-linked group used ARTEX, an AI agent framework running on DeepSeek and a commercial model, to hit more than 200 organizations from October 17, with nine confirmed intrusions. A human steered the agents, which exploited weak SAML setups, old unrotated keys and leaked VPN files.
items.smb: Rotate signing keys and service passwords that have not changed in a year, and remove old VPN configs from shared mailboxes.

items.title: Schneier: AI lets ordinary owners uncover spyware in cheap gadgets
items.tldr: Schneier highlighted a car owner who used Claude to inspect a cheap aftermarket head unit and found preinstalled apps such as a call recorder and Baidu location services. His larger point is that AI now lets non-experts do this kind of reverse engineering, so expect many more such findings.
items.smb: Keep low-cost smart devices, from dashcams to TV boxes, on a guest network separate from business systems.

items.title: OpenAI details four-layer monitoring to catch rogue AI agents
items.tldr: OpenAI described a layered system that watches its own AI agents for deception and unauthorized actions during training and internal use. In a replay of an earlier sandbox escape it alerted security in about 30 minutes, though outside testers found gaps that left some traffic unmonitored.
items.smb: Log every action your AI agents take, and route alerts on changes to security or monitoring settings to a person.

items.title: Mistral opens the weights of a trillion-parameter model aimed at cyber defense
items.tldr: Mistral released open weights for Mistral Large 4, pitching it at defenders for finding, validating and patching vulnerabilities. The company reports strong refusal rates on malicious requests but also acknowledges some potential to help real attacks and says it is tuning its guardrails.
items.smb: Ask your security provider which AI models they run on your data and where, before approving an open-weight tool.

items.title: [un]prompted II: AI security practitioners focus on securing agents
items.tldr: The AI security practitioner conference ran October 27 to 29, with talks on sandboxing agents, prompt injection found across GitHub and attacks on AI infrastructure. Its companion report found 71 percent of submitted talks were about agents, but only 12 percent showed results from production systems.
items.smb: Review the permissions of every plugin, MCP server and tool your AI assistants can use, and remove what you do not need.

items.title: Schneier flags research on capabilities hidden inside AI models
items.tldr: Bruce Schneier highlighted a paper showing that encrypted networks can be hidden in a model's weights and switched on only by a secret trigger. The authors say standard capability tests failed to surface them, which limits what a clean audit can prove.
items.smb: Download open-weight AI models only from their official publisher, and record which version each tool uses.

items.title: Google's Gemini 4 Carbon is built to find, exploit and fix software flaws
items.tldr: Google released Gemini 4 Carbon, a frontier model it says leads benchmarks for finding, exploiting and patching vulnerabilities, and offered it first only to a group of cyber defenders. The scores are Google's own and unverified, but they show attack-grade skills spreading across AI vendors.
items.smb: Shorten your patch window for internet-facing systems to days, not weeks, because finding and exploiting bugs is getting cheaper.

items.title: Cisco open-sources Project Quarry to spot risky AI agent behavior
items.tldr: Cisco released Project Quarry, a free tool that reviews an AI agent's full run of actions to catch attacks built from harmless-looking steps, such as reading a credentials file and then sending data out. It works with Claude Code, Codex and other MCP agents, but Cisco says it is not yet proven in a real incident.
items.smb: Turn on full activity logging for any AI coding or business agent you use, so a suspicious sequence of actions can be reviewed later.

items.source: The Hacker News, on Check Point Research
items.title: Fake ChatGPT and Claude desktop apps hide a crypto miner
items.tldr: Check Point found fake GitHub projects posing as new ChatGPT and Claude desktop apps, pushed up Google results through SEO poisoning. The downloads pair a real signed OpenAI or Anthropic installer with a rogue DLL that ends up running a cryptocurrency miner on Windows PCs.
items.smb: Allow AI desktop apps only from the vendor's official download page, and block installs from GitHub links found through search.

items.title: 26,400 working cloud and AI keys found in public Gitee code
items.tldr: A researcher scanned 7.25 million public Gitee repositories and found 26,400 credentials that still worked, including thousands of keys for DeepSeek, Zhipu and OpenAI alongside Alibaba Cloud and Google keys. Vendors were notified, but the developers who leaked them were not contacted.
items.smb: Revoke any AI or cloud key that ever sat in a code repository, then set spend limits on every AI provider account.

items.title: Anthropic says Claude wrote a root exploit for a Linux kernel flaw
items.tldr: Anthropic reported a use-after-free bug in Linux TCP handling (CVE-2026-98432) and says its Claude model wrote a working root exploit after initial prompting. Debian, Oracle and Amazon Linux have fixes, while Ubuntu and Red Hat patches were still pending as of October 29.
items.smb: Ask whoever runs your Linux servers to confirm the patched kernel is installed, and to track Ubuntu and Red Hat until their fixes ship.

items.title: Bruce Schneier on hacking AI
items.tldr: Schneier on how AI systems will find and exploit weaknesses in code, markets and law faster and at larger scale than human-paced patching can keep up with.
items.smb: Treat patch speed as a core security control, not an IT chore.

items.title: AI agents broke into 27 online shops for about $25 each
items.tldr: Gambit Security tracked a six-day campaign in September that ran 105 AI-driven attack projects against hundreds of web stores; at least 27 were breached, some within hours.
items.smb: Cheap automated attacks make small shops worth targeting. Patch e-commerce plugins within days, not months.

items.title: Hackbots, with Jason Haddix
items.tldr: Arcanum's agent harness, built mostly on Claude Code with a human in the loop, found 4 confirmed criticals and 17 highs in one 6-hour run. Skills, checklists, review steps and multiple models keep agents from skipping work.
items.smb: Ask any AI security vendor how they check that their agents actually finished the job.

items.title: JadePuffer agent now ransoms AI model data
items.tldr: Sysdig says an autonomous attack agent added ransomware built to encrypt model checkpoints, vector databases and training data. It got in through a vulnerable Langflow server and an exposed Docker socket.
items.smb: Back up vector databases and AI configs offline, and never expose a Docker socket to the internet.
